transcript.text: Bosch KGN34NL3AG - some days it's fine, other days it just clicks every few minutes at the back and doesn't seem to run, and the freezer starts getting soft. Then it starts working again by itself. What's going on?

That pattern isn't normal cycling. A healthy fridge-freezer clicks once when the compressor starts, then hums steadily for a while. A click every few minutes with no cooling usually means the compressor is trying to start, failing, and its thermal overload is cutting it off. It then cools down and tries again. When it eventually catches, it runs normally again, which is why it comes and goes. 1. The start relay/overload is getting tired. This is a small plastic pack clipped to the side of the compressor (the black cylinder at the bottom back). It's the commonest cause and a cheap fix.
2. The compressor is overheating because the coils or grille are dusty, or there isn't enough space round it, or the room gets warm. 3. The compressor itself is starting to stick or fail. This is less likely, but it's the expensive one, so it's worth ruling out the cheaper causes first.
4. Less commonly, a weak supply, such as running from an extension lead or a loose plug in the socket. 1. Power. Make sure it's plugged straight into a wall socket, not an extension or adaptor, and that the plug is firm. If it is on an extension, moving it to the wall and seeing it improve points to the supply.
2. Ventilation. Unplug it, pull it out gently and vacuum the dust off the coil or grille at the back and underneath. Leave a few centimetres of gap round it, then plug it back in. If it's been fine since, overheating was the problem. If the clicking spells carry on with clean coils and good space, that points to the relay or compressor.
3. Listen during a bad spell. Note whether you hear a hum or buzz for a few seconds before each click, or just the click. Also note whether the black cylinder feels very hot (touch it briefly and carefully). A hum then a click, with a hot compressor, fits the relay or compressor struggling to start.
4. While the plug is out, have a look at the side of the compressor for the relay pack. Only do this if you can see it without taking anything apart. A burnt smell or scorch marks would point strongly at it. On bad days, keep the freezer door shut and move anything important into a cool bag or another freezer if it starts to soften. Thank you, that's helpful. It is plugged straight into the wall socket, and I get the same thing on another socket. The back is a bit dusty but it does have a gap round it. On a bad day the click comes from the box on the side of the compressor, and the compressor is very hot to touch. There's no burning smell and nothing trips. What would you suggest next?

Your findings help a lot. The supply is fine, since it does the same on two sockets. The click is coming from the box on the side of the compressor, which is the start relay/overload pack, and the compressor gets very hot on bad days. That is the classic picture of the compressor trying to start, failing, and the overload cutting it off. The heat is mostly the result of those failed starts rather than the cause, because a stalled compressor heats up fast. The gap round it means ventilation is unlikely to be the main problem. In order, the likely causes are: 1. The start relay/overload is getting tired. This is the most likely cause and the cheap one.
2. The compressor itself is starting to stick. It's less likely, but it's the expensive one.
3. Dust adding a bit of extra heat. This is a minor factor at most. What I'd suggest next: 1. Clear the dust anyway. Unplug it, then vacuum the coil or grille at the back and underneath, and the area round the compressor. It's free and removes one variable. If the bad days stop after that, heat was tipping it over the edge.
2. Listen during the next bad spell. Note whether there's a hum or buzz for a few seconds before each click, or just a click on its own. - A hum then a click means the compressor is getting power but can't turn over. That can be a weak relay or a sticking compressor. - A click with no hum at all points more firmly at the relay or overload.
3. Inspect the relay pack while it's unplugged. Look only, without disconnecting anything. Check for discolouration, cracks or a melted look. If it's an obvious unclip-and-pull-off type and you're confident, you can gently shake it with the fridge unplugged. A rattle inside is a strong sign it's failed. The relay is the likely part, but it isn't confirmed yet. What would settle it is a known-good relay going on: if it then starts cleanly every time, that was the fault. If it still only hums and clicks with a good relay, the compressor is sticking, and that's a sealed-system job for an engineer. If you'd rather not touch the relay at all, a fridge engineer can test the relay and compressor windings in one visit. Ask them to check the relay first before condemning the compressor. On bad days, keep the freezer door shut and move anything precious into cool bags if it starts to soften.

I've heard it on the bad days already: there's a click, then a very brief hum, then silence for a few minutes before it clicks again. I'm not confident about taking the relay off myself, so what would you recommend I do from here?

Your click, brief hum, then a few minutes of silence is a textbook failed start. The relay clicks in, the compressor gets power and hums, but it can't turn over. The overload then cuts it off until it cools and tries again. It suggests the problem is the start side, but that sound can't tell a weak relay from a compressor that's starting to stick. Both give exactly that pattern, and only a test separates them. 1. Give the back and underneath a quick vacuum while it's unplugged, if you haven't already. It won't fix a tired relay, but it takes away any extra heat that might be making the bad days worse.
2. Book a fridge or refrigeration engineer, either Bosch's own service or a reputable independent one. Ask them to test or swap the start relay/overload first, and then check the compressor windings before condemning the compressor. That's a single visit.
3. If the relay is the fault, which is the more likely outcome, it's a cheap, quick repair and well worth doing.
4. If a known-good relay still gives just a hum and a click, the compressor is sticking. At that point replacing it is usually the sensible choice, and the engineer can advise. In the meantime, keep the freezer door shut as much as possible. On bad days, move anything important into cool bags or another freezer if it starts to soften. Don't worry about the clicking itself, because the overload is doing its job protecting the compressor. Still, the sooner it's seen, the less strain it goes through.
